n: Another famine strikes, as in Abraham’s day, and Isaac moves to Gerar under King Abimelech. Isaac’s life often echoes his father’s, showing the same God guiding a new generation.

f.w: the first famine that was in the days of Abraham

f.g: Possibly a royal title or a later king of the same name as in chapter 20.

n: The Lord appears to Isaac and tells him not to go to Egypt but to stay where God directs. Isaac, unlike Abraham and Jacob, never leaves the promised land.

f.g: Isaac remains in the land of promise all his life.

n: God promises to be with Isaac, bless him, give him the land, and fulfill the oath He swore to Abraham. The covenant is now Isaac’s.

f.w: the oath which I sware unto Abraham

n: God repeats the covenant promises to Isaac: countless descendants, the land, and blessing for all nations.

f.w: in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed

n: God says these blessings come partly because of Abraham’s obedience. Faithful parents can bless their children’s lives for generations.

f.w: my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws
f.g: A full list of terms for God’s instructions, stressing Abraham’s complete obedience.

n: Isaac settles in Gerar.
Like his father, Isaac fears for his life and says his beautiful wife is his sister. Unlike Sarah, Rebekah was his cousin, not his sister.
After a long time, Abimelech sees Isaac showing affection to Rebekah—clearly as a husband, not a brother.

f.g: Caressing or laughing with; another wordplay on Isaac’s name (“he laughs”).

n: Abimelech confronts Isaac, who admits he feared for his life.
Abimelech rebukes Isaac: someone might easily have slept with Rebekah and brought guilt on the whole nation. Again, the foreign king shows a strong moral sense.
Abimelech orders protection for Isaac and Rebekah under penalty of death. God turns Isaac’s fearful mistake into safety.
Isaac plants crops and harvests a hundred times what he sowed—an extraordinary yield in a famine. The Lord blesses him.
Isaac grows richer and richer until he is very wealthy.
His wealth in livestock and servants makes the Philistines jealous.
Out of envy, the Philistines fill in the wells Abraham’s servants had dug. In dry country, stopping a well was hostile and destructive.
Abimelech asks Isaac to leave because he has become too powerful.
Isaac moves peacefully to the valley of Gerar rather than fight.

f.g: Hebrew naḥal—a wadi or streambed that flows only in the rainy season.

n: Isaac re-digs his father’s wells and gives them the names Abraham had used. He honors and restores his father’s legacy.

f.g: Many see a parallel to restoring old truths—reopening wells of living water.

n: Isaac’s servants dig and find a well of fresh, running water.

f.g: Literally “living water”—fresh water from a spring.

n: The local herdsmen claim the water. Isaac names the well Esek, “quarrel.”
They dig another well, and that one too is disputed. Isaac names it Sitnah, “opposition.”

f.g: Means “hostility” or “accusation”; related to the word “Satan.”

n: Isaac moves on and digs another well that no one disputes. He names it Rehoboth, “room,” praising the Lord for making space for them. Patience and peacemaking are rewarded.

f.w: the LORD hath made room for us

n: Isaac then moves up to Beersheba.
That night the Lord appears, introducing Himself as the God of Abraham, and comforts Isaac with “fear not.” He promises His presence and blessing.

f.w: I am the God of Abraham thy father

n: Isaac responds as Abraham did: he builds an altar, calls on the Lord, pitches his tent, and digs a well. Worship comes first.
Abimelech comes with his adviser and army commander, the same kind of delegation that came to Abraham.
Isaac asks why they come now, after showing hostility and driving him away.
They admit they have seen that the Lord is with Isaac, so they want a peace treaty. Isaac’s faithfulness has become a witness to outsiders.
They ask Isaac to promise not to harm them, claiming they treated him only with kindness—a generous description of events.

f.w: thou art now the blessed of the LORD
f.g: An acknowledgment of God’s favor on Isaac.

n: Isaac hosts a feast. Sharing a meal often sealed covenants in the ancient world.
Early the next morning they swear the oath, and Isaac sends them away in peace.
That same day his servants report that they have found water—a sign of God’s approval of the peace.

f.g: A timely blessing right after making peace.

n: Isaac names the well Shibah (“oath”), renewing the name Beersheba. The narrator ties the city’s name to both Abraham and Isaac.
At forty, Esau marries two Hittite women. This shows his disregard for covenant marriage, as Abraham had insisted Isaac not marry Canaanites.

f.g: The same age at which Isaac married (25:20).

n: Esau’s marriages cause bitter grief to Isaac and Rebekah. This prepares for Rebekah’s concern that Jacob marry within the covenant.
